title: Review: your second week, from Brent to forward curves
story: Friday evening, week two. Sam puts six sticky notes on your screen: Brent, Platts, TTF, power, EUAs, curve. *"Six markets in six days. Tonight, no new words. Tell me how they fit together, then value one small book for me, like you will do every evening."*
objective: I can connect the six markets of week two and use them to value a small book.

write.heading: 1. The week in six lines
write.body:
- **L8**: oil benchmarks Brent, WTI, Dubai; price = benchmark ± differential (→ L8).
- **L9**: Platts and Argus publish price assessments used in contracts and MtM (→ L9).
- **L10**: gas hubs TTF (EUR/MWh), NBP (p/therm), Henry Hub (USD/MMBtu), JKM (→ L10).
- **L11**: power: day-ahead, intraday, baseload, peakload; MW × hours = MWh (→ L11).
- **L12**: carbon: EU ETS, 1 EUA = 1 t CO2 (→ L12).
- **L13**: forward curve: one price per tenor (→ L13).

write.heading: 2. Mini case: Dana's small book
write.body: Example (illustrative): Dana bought 10 MW of German baseload power for January. January has 31 days, so 10 × 24 × 31 = **7,440 MWh**. Dana bought at 90 EUR/MWh. Tonight the January tenor of the power curve closes at 95. MtM = (95 − 90) × 7,440 = **+37,200 EUR**.

write.heading: 3. What you check first
write.body: Is the unit right (MWh, not MW)? Is the curve tenor January, not spot? Is the closing price from the right source? One wrong answer, and the P&L is wrong.

check.q: A crude is sold at "Dated Brent minus 1.50". What is Dated Brent here, and who publishes it?
check.a: It is the benchmark price; the 1.50 USD/bbl is the differential. Dated Brent is a price assessment published by a price reporting agency such as Platts (L8, L9).

check.q: Give the unit of TTF and of Henry Hub. Why is this a trap in a report?
check.a: TTF: EUR/MWh. Henry Hub: USD/MMBtu. Different currency and energy unit, so the two numbers cannot be compared or added directly (L10).

check.q: 5 MW baseload for one day: how many MWh?
Why do power traders also watch the EUA price?
check.a: A gas or coal plant must surrender EUAs for its CO2, so carbon is part of the cost of producing power (L12).

read_more: Flip back through L8 to L13 while you copy: each (→ L<n>) mark is a page to reread. The January power numbers are illustrative only. Note that the case values only the open trade with the curve, exactly as in L13: next lesson looks at the shape of that curve, contango and backwardation.
next: Next lesson (L15): contango and backwardation, the two shapes of a forward curve and what they tell you.
